text: It's ridiculous. I would say that by the time we are done recording this podcast, I'll have, I don't know. I mean, it could be anywhere from 30 to 50 pitches in my inbox. It comes all day.
speaker: Jason Feifer
context: Lenny asks Jason about the volume of pitches he receives from startup founders and PR people trying to get coverage. Jason is explaining the overwhelming amount of press pitches he receives daily as editor-in-chief of Entrepreneur Magazine. He emphasizes that most pitches are mass-distributed, irrelevant press releases rather than targeted, thoughtful outreach.
text_ko: 말도 안 돼요. 이 팟캐스트 녹음이 끝날 때쯤이면 제 인박스에… 글쎄요, 대략 30개에서 50개 정도의 피치(pitch)가 와 있을 거예요. 하루 종일 계속 들어와요.
text_zh: 太夸张了。我估计等我们把这期播客录完，我收件箱里大概会有——我也说不准——三十到五十封推介邮件（pitch）。整天都有。
text_es: Es ridículo. Diría que para cuando terminemos de grabar este podcast me habrán llegado —no sé— entre 30 y 50 propuestas (pitches) a la bandeja de entrada. Me llegan todo el día.
original_text: It's ridiculous. I would say that by the time we are done recording this podcast, I'll have, I don't know. I mean, it could be anywhere from 30 to 50 pitches in my inbox. It comes all day. Now, to be clear, most of that is garbage in the real garbagey sense, right. It's a lot of completely unrelevant press releases that were sent to me and a bazillion other people.

vocabulary.definition: Proposals or presentations made to persuade someone to buy a product, invest in a project, or support an idea.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the startup ecosystem, 'pitches' are crucial for entrepreneurs seeking funding, as they must effectively communicate their business model and value proposition to potential investors.
vocabulary.nuance: The term can imply a sense of urgency or competition, as multiple pitches may be vying for attention and approval.

text: And that means that you could end up... I write this newsletter, right. I have... Entrepreneur Magazine is the thing that people obviously would pitch, but then I have this newsletter where I don't interview anybody.
speaker: Jason Feifer
context: Jason explains how automated PR systems work poorly for entrepreneurs. He describes how PR agencies often add publications to spreadsheets without understanding what they actually cover. Jason uses his own newsletter as an example - it doesn't feature interviews or stories about companies, yet he still receives irrelevant pitches because someone added it to a database without researching its format or purpose.
text_ko: 그러면 결국 그렇게 될 수도 있어요… 저는 이 뉴스레터를 쓰잖아요. 사람들은 당연히 Entrepreneur Magazine에 제안하라고 하겠지만, 저는 아무도 인터뷰하지 않는 뉴스레터를 운영하고 있어요.
text_zh: 那就是说，你可能会变成这样……我写这份邮件简报 (newsletter)，对吧。我还有别的渠道，大家通常会把内容投给《Entrepreneur》杂志 (Entrepreneur Magazine)，但我的这份简报里根本没有采访环节。
text_es: Y eso quiere decir que al final puedes acabar así: escribo este boletín (newsletter), ¿no? También colaboro con Entrepreneur Magazine —esa es la opción que la gente, obviamente, propondría (pitch)— pero en mi boletín no hago entrevistas a nadie.
key_sentence: And that means that you could end up...
original_text: And that means that you could end up... I write this newsletter, right. I have... Entrepreneur Magazine is the thing that people obviously would pitch, but then I have this newsletter where I don't interview anybody. There's no opportunity to be featured in my newsletter, and I still get pitches to the newsletter because somebody saw it and dropped it in some spreadsheet, and it just... now I get it. And I think that's a real disservice to entrepreneurs who are paying for people to do that, and I really hate that.

vocabulary.definition: A persuasive presentation or proposal aimed at convincing an audience to support an idea, product, or service.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the startup ecosystem, a pitch is often delivered to investors or stakeholders to secure funding or partnerships, highlighting the value proposition and potential return on investment.
vocabulary.nuance: The term 'pitch' can imply a sense of urgency or salesmanship, which may not always be appropriate in more formal or collaborative discussions.

text: Think about press the same way that you think about raising money, which is to say you do it when you know what the money is for, and you should do it when you know what the press is for.
speaker: Jason Feifer
context: Lenny asks Jason when it's worth investing time in getting press coverage. Jason draws a parallel between seeking press and fundraising, emphasizing that both should be pursued strategically when you have a clear purpose. He explains that many entrepreneurs seek press too early in their company's development, when coverage wouldn't actually benefit their business goals or stage.
text_ko: 언론(press)은 자금 조달(raising money)을 생각하는 방식 그대로 접근해 보세요. 즉, 돈을 무엇에 쓸지 분명할 때만 모금을 하는 것처럼, 언론도 그것을 통해 얻고자 하는 목적이 분명할 때만 활용해야 해요.
text_zh: 把媒体(press)当成融资(raising money)那样对待：只有在清楚钱要用在哪儿才去融资，同样只有在清楚媒体能帮你做什么才去找媒体。
text_es: Piensa en la prensa como piensas en levantar financiación: lo haces cuando sabes para qué vas a usar el dinero; con la prensa deberías actuar igual —búscala solo cuando tengas claro qué quieres conseguir con ella.
key_sentence: you should do it when you know what the press is for.
original_text: Think about press the same way that you think about raising money, which is to say you do it when you know what the money is for, and you should do it when you know what the press is for. A lot of people reach out to me at such an early stage that if we wrote about them, it wouldn't get them anything. They're not at a stage where they could use that press in any meaningful way, and so there's really no purpose in chasing it now.

text: But I get a lot of emails. It's funny because people are... like entrepreneurs, in particular, they're just so vulnerable, and it's kind of a wonderful way sometimes.
speaker: Jason Feifer
context: Jason continues explaining when it makes sense to pursue press coverage. He describes the emotional vulnerability of entrepreneurs who sometimes reach out saying they 'deserve' press coverage after working hard. While Jason empathizes with this feeling, he emphasizes that deserving coverage isn't a strategic business reason that will actually help achieve meaningful goals.
text_ko: 근데 이메일이 정말 많이 와요. 웃긴 건, 사람들—특히 창업가들(entrepreneurs)은 정말 취약하다는 거예요. 그래서 그게 가끔은 오히려 참 좋은 방식이 되더라고요.
text_zh: 我收到很多邮件。说来有趣的是，尤其是企业家(entrepreneurs)，他们挺脆弱的，有时候这反而挺好的。
text_es: Pero recibo muchos correos (emails). Lo curioso es que la gente —y en particular los emprendedores— se muestran muy vulnerables, y a veces eso es algo maravilloso.
key_sentence: entrepreneurs, in particular, they're just so vulnerable, and it's kind of a wonderful way sometimes.
original_text: But I get a lot of emails. It's funny because people are... like entrepreneurs, in particular, they're just so vulnerable, and it's kind of a wonderful way sometimes. And sometimes people will just email me, and they'll just say, "You know, I've worked really hard, and I just feel like I deserve this." I respect that, and I relate to it in some ways with my own trying to get attention for my own work. But, "I deserve this" that's not a good tactical decision for your business that doesn't do anything for you.

vocabulary.definition: Open to emotional or physical harm; susceptible to being hurt or attacked.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, being vulnerable can refer to the challenges entrepreneurs face when exposing their ideas or emotions, which can lead to both innovation and risk.
vocabulary.nuance: While vulnerability can be seen as a weakness, it often signifies authenticity and the potential for deeper connections in professional relationships.

vocabulary.definition: Individuals who start and manage their own businesses, taking on financial risks in the hope of profit.
vocabulary.businessContext: Entrepreneurs are often at the forefront of innovation and economic growth, driving new ideas and solutions in various industries.
vocabulary.nuance: The term often carries a connotation of ambition and creativity, but it can also imply a level of uncertainty and risk-taking.

vocabulary.definition: Inspiring delight, pleasure, or admiration; excellent or remarkable.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, describing a product or service as wonderful can indicate high quality and customer satisfaction, often used in marketing.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'wonderful' conveys strong positive feelings, it may come across as overly subjective or informal in certain professional communications.

text: So that means that 99.5% of the people who would read a story about this guy have no ability to go get his hotdogs, which means that that was wasted effort. So fine.
speaker: Jason Feifer
context: Jason tells the story of a hot dog food truck owner in Washington DC who wanted coverage in Entrepreneur Magazine. Jason explains why this would be ineffective - Entrepreneur has a national/international audience, but the hot dog vendor can only serve local customers. Jason uses this example to illustrate how entrepreneurs often target the wrong publications that don't reach their actual customer base.
text_ko: 그러니까 이 사람 이야기를 읽을 사람 중 99.5%는 그의 핫도그를 사러 갈 수 있는 여건이 안 된다는 얘기고, 결국 그건 헛수고였어요. 그럼 됐어요.
text_zh: 也就是说，读到关于这个人的故事的99.5%的人根本没法去买他的热狗，所以那就是白白浪费力气。好吧，算了。
text_es: Eso quiere decir que el 99,5% de la gente que leería una historia sobre este tipo no tiene forma de ir a comprar sus perros calientes, así que todo ese esfuerzo fue inútil. Pues ya está.
key_sentence: 99.5% of the people who would read a story about this guy have no ability to go get his hotdogs.
original_text: So that means that 99.5% of the people who would read a story about this guy have no ability to go get his hotdogs, which means that that was wasted effort. So fine. Was it that hard to come up and talk to me at the conference? No. But scale that out. How many emails is he sending that are like that? How much energy is he putting into chasing things that ultimately don't have good direct value to him?

vocabulary.definition: An attempt or action that yields no productive results or benefits, often due to misalignment with goals or audience needs.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, wasted effort refers to resources expended on initiatives that do not contribute to strategic objectives, often leading to inefficiencies and lost opportunities.
vocabulary.nuance: This phrase carries a negative connotation, suggesting that the effort could have been better utilized elsewhere.

vocabulary.definition: The capacity or skill to perform a task or action; often related to an individual's competence or potential.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the business world, ability is crucial for assessing employee performance, team dynamics, and the overall capability to achieve organizational goals.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'ability' typically refers to inherent skills, it can also encompass learned competencies, making it a versatile term in various contexts.

text: They don't care about you. They don't care about you. They care about their reader or their listener or their viewer. That's who they care about.
speaker: Jason Feifer
context: Jason explains a fundamental misunderstanding entrepreneurs have about media. Many people approach journalists and editors as if they're service providers whose job is to give coverage. Jason clarifies that media professionals' primary loyalty is to their audience, not to the people pitching them stories. He emphasizes that successful pitches must demonstrate value to the publication's readers rather than just promoting the entrepreneur's business.
text_ko: 그들은 당신에게 관심 없어요. 진짜예요. 그들이 신경 쓰는 건 독자나 청자, 시청자예요.
text_zh: 他们不在乎你，真的不在乎。他们在乎的是读者、听众或观众，那才是他们真正关心的对象。
text_es: A ellos no les importas. A ellos no les importas. Lo que les importa es su lector, su oyente o su espectador.
key_sentence: They care about their reader or their listener or their viewer.
original_text: They don't care about you. They don't care about you. They care about their reader or their listener or their viewer. That's who they care about. That's who they're serving, and if you can be of use to them in sharing the kinds of information that they are looking to serve their audience, then you can get what you want. But you can't treat them like a service provider because they're not.

text: So when people would pitch what we'd really be looking for are, are there insights into...
speaker: Jason Feifer
context: Jason explains the editorial mission differences between publications, using his experience at Fast Company as an example. When he worked at Fast Company under editor-in-chief Bob Safian, the magazine focused on where business was heading and evolution of industries. Jason describes what made stories appealing to Fast Company - they needed to provide insights that would help readers understand industry trends and adapt their own companies accordingly.
text_ko: 사람들이 제안할 때, 우리가 진짜로 찾고 있는 건 …에 대한 인사이트가 있느냐 하는 거예요.
text_zh: 所以别人来推介时，我们真正想知道的是，是否对……有什么见解？
text_es: Así que cuando la gente venía a presentar (pitch), lo que realmente buscábamos era saber si había perspectivas (insights) sobre...
original_text: So when people would pitch what we'd really be looking for are, are there insights into... in what this person is doing that other people could read and say, "Aha, that helps me understand where this industry is going or that industry, or it helps me think about how I can shape my own company to match current trends," that kind of stuff.

vocabulary.definition: A pitch is a persuasive presentation or proposal aimed at convincing an audience to support an idea, product, or service.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and startup environments, pitches are often delivered to potential investors, clients, or partners to secure funding or collaboration.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'pitch' can refer to any form of presentation, it often implies a degree of enthusiasm and urgency, making it more suitable in informal or dynamic settings.

vocabulary.definition: Insights are deep understandings or revelations about a particular subject, often derived from data analysis or experiential knowledge.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, insights are crucial for making informed decisions, driving strategy, and identifying market opportunities based on consumer behavior or trends.
vocabulary.nuance: The term 'insights' carries a connotation of depth and clarity, suggesting that the information provided is not just surface-level but offers significant value.
